files.lesson.md: --- order: 5 unit: models10 node: AC9M10A04 n1 uses: [AC9M10A03 n1, AC9M9A05 n1] # a constant ratio; choosing a line or a quadratic by differences (Year 9) connection: car-value title: Which model? summary: "Look at a table and decide: equal differences mean a line, equal second differences mean a quadratic, an equal ratio means an exponential. Then say which pattern you found." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Used cars get cheaper every year. How cheap, by how old?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8386 url: http://127.0.0.1:8386/index.html readySelector: "#sl-m" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: model.yml#explain-pic, caption: "The dots are the prices. The dashed line drops the same dollars each year and misses them. The solid curve takes 20% off each year and passes through all five." } explainClip: query: { code: "@model.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Two models, one set of prices" say: "Two models, one set of prices." clip: - caption: { text: "The dots are the prices. The dashed line takes off the same dollars each year.", say: "The dots are the prices. The dashed line takes off the same dollars every year." } - wait: 600 - click: Make b smaller - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "The solid curve takes off the same share each year.", say: "The solid curve takes off the same share each year." } - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Only one of them goes through every dot.", say: "Only one of them goes through every dot." } - wait: 1200 --- A dealer lists the same model of car at different ages. The prices below are made up for this lesson. Real prices also depend on kilometres and condition. | Age (years) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | |---|---|---|---|---| | Price ($) | 30,000 | 24,000 | 19,200 | 15,360 | ## Predict: the 4-year-old car ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the next price shows who repeats the last drop in dollars (11,520) and who sees the price falling by the same share each year (12,288)." check: type: predict q: "The same model is for sale at 0, 1, 2 and 3 years old for the prices above. What would you expect a 4-year-old one to cost?" options: - "$12{,}288" - "$11{,}520" - "$12{,}000" - "$9{,}000" actual: "12,288. The drops are 6,000, then 4,800, then 3,840: they get smaller. Each price is 0.8 times the one before (24,000 ÷ 30,000 = 0.8, 19,200 ÷ 24,000 = 0.8), so 15,360 × 0.8 = 12,288. Taking off 3,840 again would give 11,520, which is a line's answer." ``` The bars show the prices from new to 3 years old. Make a guess before you check. ## Run: line or curve ```step stage: run insight: "A straight-line model drops the same dollars every year; an exponential model drops the same share every year. Only one of them goes through all the dots." try: { playground: board, starter: "model.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "The dots are the prices. Set $b$ to 0.8 so the solid curve passes through them. Read the table at 4 years. Does it match your prediction?", when: "b = 0.8" } ``` The solid curve multiplies the price by $b$ each year. The dashed line takes the same dollars off each year, set by $m$. Try to get the dashed line through all five dots too. ## Investigate: differences or ratios ```step stage: investigate insight: "Three tests sort a table: equal first differences (a line), equal second differences (a quadratic) and an equal ratio (an exponential). Dev sees the price falling and calls it a line without testing." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Look at $64, 48, 36, 27$. What do you multiply by to get from each value to the next?" answer: "0.75" feedback: - ["-16", "That's 48 − 64, how far it falls. The ratio is what you multiply by: 48 ÷ 64."] - ["0.25", "That's the share it drops by. Multiply by 0.75 to keep the other 75%."] explain: "48 ÷ 64 = 0.75, 36 ÷ 48 = 0.75 and 27 ÷ 36 = 0.75. Each value is 0.75 times the one before." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#dev" text: "Dev looks at the car prices. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: decay-means-linear explain: "Line 2: falling every year doesn't make a table linear. A line drops the same dollars each time. These drops are 6,000, 4,800 and 3,840, so they aren't the same. The ratio is 0.8 every time, so it's exponential, and the table was right." - check: type: question q: "Which table is exponential?" options: ["$100, 90, 80, 70$", "$100, 90, 81, 72.9$", "$100, 90, 70, 40$"] answer: 1 feedback: ["That takes off 10 every time. It's linear.", null, "The drops are 10, 20, 30: the second differences are equal (10), so it's a quadratic."] explain: "100, 90, 81, 72.9: each value is 0.9 times the one before." ``` ### Multiply by what? There are three tests, and you try them in order. ```worked 10,\; 12,\; 14.4,\; 17.28 :: Which model fits this table? 2,\; 2.4,\; 2.88 :: First differences. They aren't equal, so it isn't a line. 0.4,\; 0.48 :: Second differences. They aren't equal either, so it isn't a quadratic. 12 \div 10,\; 14.4 \div 12,\; 17.28 \div 14.4 :: Ratios. 1.2,\; 1.2,\; 1.2 :: The same every time. \text{exponential, ratio } 1.2 :: Equal ratios mean exponential. Each value is 1.2 times the one before. ``` Now try one on paper: $64, 48, 36, 27$. Find the ratio, then type it. ### Find the mistake Read Dev's working. Which line decides without testing? ### Which table? Look for the same ratio. ## Modify: change the car ```step stage: modify insight: "A model can be tested against more data. A line can run below zero where the price can't, while an exponential falls but never reaches it." try: { playground: board, starter: "model.yml#vary", height: 640 } tasks: - hint: ["Set $b$ to 0.7 and read the table at 2 years ($x = 2$).", "$30000 \\times 0.7 \\times 0.7$."] check: { type: answer, q: "A different car loses 30% of its price each year, so $b = 0.7$. Starting from $30,000$, what is its price at 2 years?", answer: "14700", feedback: [["21000", "That's the price after 1 year. Multiply by 0.7 again."], ["12000", "That takes 30% off twice from the start in dollars. Multiply by 0.7 twice instead."]], explain: "30,000 × 0.7 = 21,000, and 21,000 × 0.7 = 14,700." } - hint: ["Put 7 into the dashed line's rule.", "$30000 - 4800 \\times 7$."] check: { type: answer, q: "The dashed line is $y = 30000 - 4800x$. What does it give at 7 years?", answer: "-3600", feedback: [["3600", "30,000 − 33,600 is below zero. Keep the minus sign."], ["26400", "That's 30,000 − 3,600. The rule takes off 4,800 for each year, so 7 years takes off 33,600."]], explain: "4,800 × 7 = 33,600, and 30,000 − 33,600 = −3,600." } - hint: "Slide $b$ to 1 and watch the table." check: type: question q: "Edge case: set $b$ to 1. What are the difference and the ratio between neighbouring prices?" options: ["The difference is 0 and the ratio is 1: the price never changes", "The difference is 1 and the ratio is 0", "The price drops to 0"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Swapped: nothing is taken off, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing.", "A ratio of 1 keeps the price at 30,000."] explain: "Multiplying by 1 changes nothing, so the table is flat. It is both a line (difference 0) and an exponential (ratio 1)." ``` ### Another car Each task changes the board or the rule. Answer from the table. ### Below zero ### A ratio of 1 ## Practise: choose the model ```step stage: practise insight: "Testing a table for a line, a quadratic and an exponential in order, and (review) solving an equation with x in the power." tasks: - check: type: question q: "A table gives $6, 9, 13.5, 20.25$. Which model fits?" options: ["Exponential: each value is 1.5 times the one before", "Linear: the differences are equal", "Quadratic: the second differences are equal", "None of them"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The differences are 3, 4.5, 6.75: not equal.", "The first differences are 3, 4.5, 6.75 and the second differences are 1.5, 2.25: not equal.", "The ratio is 1.5 every time."] explain: "9 ÷ 6 = 1.5, 13.5 ÷ 9 = 1.5 and 20.25 ÷ 13.5 = 1.5." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Just one step: how many times bigger is 9 than 6?", answer: 1.5, explain: "9 ÷ 6 = 1.5. Check it against 13.5 ÷ 9." } - check: type: question q: "A table gives $3, 7, 13, 21$. Which model fits?" options: ["Quadratic: the second differences are both 2", "Linear: the differences are equal", "Exponential: the ratios are equal", "None of them"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The differences are 4, 6, 8: not equal.", "The ratios are 2.33, 1.86 and 1.62: not equal.", "The second differences are 2 and 2, so a quadratic fits exactly."] explain: "First differences 4, 6, 8. Second differences 2, 2." - check: type: question q: "A table gives $50, 45, 40, 35$. Which model fits?" options: ["Linear: it takes off 5 every time", "Exponential: it falls every time", "Quadratic: it falls every time", "None of them"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Falling isn't enough. The ratios are 0.9, 0.89, 0.875: not equal.", "The second differences are 0: the first differences are already equal.", "A line fits exactly."] explain: "The differences are −5, −5, −5. Equal differences mean a line." - check: type: number q: "Review: solve $2^x = 32$. What is $x$?" answer: 5 explain: "32 = 2⁵, so the bases match and x = 5." ``` ### A multiplying table ### A second difference ### A falling line ### Review From the last unit: solving with the same base. ## Make: back to the car ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the car: the line through the first two prices misses the 4-year-old car by thousands, which is why checking the pattern matters." tasks: - hint: ["A line through the first two prices drops 6,000 each year.", "The exponential model gives 12,288 at 4 years."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A line through the first two prices ($30,000$ and $24,000$) drops $6,000$ each year. The exponential model says a 4-year-old car costs $12,288$. How many dollars lower is the line's price at 4 years?" steps: - ["$30000 - 6000 \\times 4 = 6000$", "what the line says at 4 years"] - ["$12288 - 6000 = 6288$", "the exponential price minus the line's price"] - ["$6288", "the line's price is $6,288 lower"] answer: "6288" answerLabel: "Dollars lower" tolerance: 0.5 feedback: - ["6000", "That's the line's price at 4 years. Subtract it from 12,288."] - ["12288", "That's the exponential price. Find how far the line's price is below it."] criteria: - "I worked out the line's price at 4 years first." - "I subtracted in the right order." - "I gave the answer in dollars." explain: "The line says 6,000 and the exponential model says 12,288. The difference is 6,288." - check: type: question q: "A buyer fits a model to five prices from a dealer's site. What else would you want to check before trusting it for every car of that model?" options: ["The kilometres and condition: the model only uses age, and they also change a price", "Nothing: a model that fits five prices is exact", "That the table only has whole numbers", "That the graph goes through (0, 0)"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A model that fits some prices isn't exact. Other things change the price too.", "Whole numbers aren't the point; the pattern is.", "A price is not 0 when the car is new."] explain: "The model uses only age. Kilometres and condition also change a price, so test it against more listings." ``` ### How far out? Back to the car. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### What else changes the price? The prices here are made up, and so is the 20% a year. Real listings differ in kilometres and condition. Your class can pick a model on a car-sales site, write down the prices at five ages and test them in the same three ways. Sources: all prices and the 20% a year are made up for this lesson. **Also used in** - **Money.** Phones, laptops and bikes lose value by a share each year, not by the same dollars. - **Science.** A table of measurements can be tested the same way: equal differences, equal second differences or an equal ratio. - **Next lesson.** Writing the rule for an exponential, then using it to answer a question in dollars. ```teacher summary: "Students test tables for a line, a quadratic and an exponential using differences, second differences and ratios, and say which pattern they found. The hinge node: classify, then justify (AC9M10A04, node 1)." time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can tell a line, a quadratic and an exponential apart from a table. - I can show the pattern that proves my choice. - I can say what a model leaves out. struggle: Choosing from the look of the numbers ('it goes down, so it's a line'). Ask 'what test did you try?' and have them write the differences and the ratio under the table before they choose. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need the exponential ratio (lesson 1) and difference and second-difference tests from Year 9 (Linear or quadratic?). The hinge: students must decide AND justify. The three tests go in order: first differences (line), second differences (quadratic), ratios (exponential). Marks go to showing the constant pattern, not to naming the model. All car prices are made up: 30,000 new and 20% off each year. Say so in class. Real listings also depend on kilometres, condition and the market. A class option: each group picks one model on a car-sales site, writes down five asking prices at different ages and tests them. Expect a rough fit, not an exact one; that is the lesson. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands before revealing. Those who chose 11,520 repeated the last drop; don't correct it yet." - "Run: ask where the dashed line and the dots separate, and what the solid curve does differently." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the dollars gap in Make are worked on paper first. Look for the ratio written as a division, not a subtraction." - "Modify: before the ratio of 1, ask what multiplying by 1 does." stuck: - see: A student says the table is a line because the price 'goes down by about the same amount'. ask: What are the drops, written out? 6,000, then what? fix: Write the three drops and the three ratios under the table. Drops 6,000, 4,800, 3,840 are not equal; ratios 0.8, 0.8, 0.8 are. - see: A student divides the wrong way (24,000 ÷ 30,000 versus 30,000 ÷ 24,000). ask: Is each price bigger or smaller than the one before? Should the ratio be bigger or smaller than 1? fix: Divide each value by the one before it. A falling table has a ratio below 1. - see: A student tests only one pair and decides. ask: Does the next pair give the same answer? fix: A pattern needs at least three values and two equal gaps or ratios. stretch: "Find a table that is both a line and an exponential. Then find one that is a quadratic and not an exponential. Real prices rarely fit exactly: how close does the exponential fit your class's real listings?" support: "A table with two extra rows: 'difference' and 'ratio'. Fill both for 2, 4, 6, 8 and for 2, 4, 8, 16 so the contrast is visible before they classify." leads: > Next: writing the model, y = a(bⁿ), with an initial value and a growth or decay factor, and using it to answer a question in dollars. Where it leads in class: judging how well a model fits real data, and what it leaves out. exit: q: A table goes 80, 100, 125, 156.25. Linear, quadratic or exponential? Show the test. a: "Exponential: 100 ÷ 80 = 1.25, 125 ÷ 100 = 1.25 and 156.25 ÷ 125 = 1.25. The differences 20, 25, 31.25 are not equal." explain: > To choose a model from a table, test it three ways, in order: 1. **First differences.** If they are equal, it's a line. 2. **Second differences** (differences of the differences). If they are equal, it's a quadratic. 3. **Ratios.** Divide each value by the one before. If they are equal, it's an exponential. Say which test worked, and show the numbers. sources: - title: "Made up for this lesson: the car prices (30,000 new, 20% off each year) are not real listings. Real prices also depend on kilometres and condition." url: https://tutorials.learningwaypoints.com/maths/functions/which-model/ checked: 2026-10-25 ```

# Boards for "Which model?". x is the age of the car in years. The dots are made-up advertised prices for one model
# of car (new, then 1, 2, 3 and 4 years old). The dashed line is a straight-line model, the solid curve an exponential one.

# region: run
widget: graph
x: 0, 6
y: 0, 32000
grid: 1, 8000
axes: Age (years), Price ($)
slider m: -8000, 0, -3000, 500
slider b: 0.5, 1, 0.9, 0.05
series Prices: 0,30000; 1,24000; 2,19200; 3,15360; 4,12288
plot: y = 30000(b^x)
plot: y = 30000 + mx, dashed
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: graph
x: 0, 6
y: 0, 32000
grid: 1, 8000
axes: Age (years), Price ($)
slider m: -8000, 0, -3000, 500
slider b: 0.5, 1, 0.9, 0.05
series Prices: 0,30000; 1,24000; 2,19200; 3,15360; 4,12288
plot: y = 30000(b^x)
plot: y = 30000 + mx, dashed
table: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: graph
x: 0, 6
y: 0, 32000
grid: 1, 8000

series Prices: 0,30000; 1,24000; 2,19200; 3,15360; 4,12288

plot: y = 30000 - 6000x, dashed

# Dev's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: dev
The prices are 30000, 24000, 19200, 15360. Is it linear or exponential?
The price goes down every year, so it's a straight line going down.
The line is y = 30000 - 6000x.
At 3 years that gives 12000, but the table says 15360. The table must be wrong.
# endregion
